Record commits for an integrity monitor

Commit records - agents name the commits they made on session_end and tasks_update, and the daemon writes a snapshot of its sessions, tasks and those commits that an integrity monitor matches a branch's commits against.

On this page
  • Turn it on
  • Recording commits
  • The snapshot
  • Which repository a session is in
  • What it does not cover

An integrity monitor watching a repository's main branch wants to know which commits came from tracked work and which came from nowhere: a commit pushed from outside every agent session and every task is the one worth a look. Seamless already knows which sessions ran when, and in which repository, and which tasks exist. Commit records let it say so, in two halves:

  1. Agents record their commits. session_end and tasks_update take an optional commits argument: the full ids of the commits a session made or a task's work produced, recorded on that session or task.
  2. The daemon writes a snapshot. One JSON file, replaced whole every few minutes, lists the sessions live in a window - name, repository, start and end - and the tasks a commit in it may name, each with the commits it recorded. The monitor reads that file and matches its own list of the branch's commits against it.

Both are off by default, and off is exactly the previous behavior: neither tool offers the argument (a call that sends one is refused as an unknown parameter, word for word as before), nothing is recorded, and no file is written. They switch on separately: a snapshot without recorded commits still tells a monitor which sessions ran when, and where.

Turn it on

commits:
  record: true                                               # offer the commits argument
  snapshot_file: /path/to/outbox/snapshot-seamless_feed.json # write the snapshot here
  snapshot_interval: 5m                                      # default 5m, from 30s to 24h
  snapshot_window: 720h                                      # default 30 days, from 1h to a year

Each key has an environment override: SEAMLESS_COMMITS_RECORD, SEAMLESS_COMMITS_SNAPSHOT_FILE, SEAMLESS_COMMITS_SNAPSHOT_INTERVAL and SEAMLESS_COMMITS_SNAPSHOT_WINDOW. They are read at start, so restart the daemon after a change. snapshot_file must be absolute (a leading ~ expands), and its directory must already exist: the daemon creates nothing there but that file (and, for a moment, a hidden temporary file beside it).

Recording commits

With record on, both tools list commits in their schema:

  • session_end commits=[...] records the ids on the session being ended - the same session the call completes, behind the same project fence.
  • tasks_update id=<task> commits=[...] records them on the task. Recording is an update like any other: it lands in the same transaction as the rest of the call, and a task another session holds via a live claim refuses it with already claimed, exactly as it refuses a retitle.

The argument takes an array, or a comma-separated string. Each entry must be a full commit id - the 40-character SHA-1 or 64-character SHA-256 name git rev-parse HEAD prints. An abbreviation is refused, never expanded: it can name a different commit once the repository grows a colliding prefix. Uppercase is read as lowercase, and a repeat counts once - within the call, and against what the session or task already holds. One call records at most 256 distinct ids, and one session or task holds at most 10,000. Any bad entry refuses the whole call: a refused session_end leaves the session open, and a refused tasks_update changes nothing, its other fields included.

A successful call reports commits_recorded, and its event (session.ended, task.transition) carries the same count. The ids themselves live in the record, never in an event.

The snapshot

With snapshot_file set, the daemon writes the snapshot as it starts and every snapshot_interval after. Each write builds the whole document, checks it against the contract below, writes it beside the file and renames it into place, so a reader never sees half of one. A snapshot that would break the contract is not written, and the last good file stays. The file's mode is 0640: put it in a directory only the daemon's account can write and whose group is the monitor's. Whoever can write that directory can replace the snapshot, and with it vouch for any commit.

{
  "kind": "seamless_feed",
  "version": 1,
  "host": "build-host",
  "taken_at": "2026-11-02T01:16:54.977Z",
  "since": "2026-10-03T01:16:54.977Z",
  "sessions": [
    {"id": "cc/0a1b2c3d-4e5f6a7b", "repo": "myapp", "started_at": "2026-11-01T09:00:00.000Z",
     "ended_at": "2026-11-01T10:30:00.000Z",
     "commits": ["1111111111111111111111111111111111111111"]},
    {"id": "cx/0f0f0f0f-1e1e1e1e", "repo": null, "started_at": "2026-11-02T01:00:00.000Z",
     "ended_at": null}
  ],
  "tasks": [
    {"id": "01ARZ3NDEKTSV4RRFFQ69G5FAV", "repo": "myapp",
     "commits": ["2222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222222"]}
  ]
}
Field What it holds
host The daemon's host name, lowercase
taken_at When it was built, UTC to the millisecond
since The start of what it covers: snapshot_window before taken_at, or the start of the first session when that is later. A commit seen before it is outside the snapshot
sessions[].id The session's name - the cc/... or cx/... on a briefing's Seam session line, or a sess/* name - so a commit message that mentions it matches. A name outside the contract's pattern is replaced by the session's ULID
sessions[].repo The repository the session's working directory is in, or null
sessions[].started_at, ended_at When it started, and when it ended - null while it is active. A session idle longer than gardener.session_idle_minutes has ended at its last activity, the end the idle reaper gives it: never at the moment it was reaped, and whether or not the reaper runs
tasks[].id A task's ULID, for a commit message that names one
tasks[].repo Its project's repository, when the project maps exactly one; left out otherwise
commits The ids recorded on the session or task, oldest first; left out when there are none

Which entries it lists: every session live at some point since since, and every task that is open or in progress or changed since since (closing a task and recording its commits both change it). Up to 100,000 of each: past that, the sessions that ended earliest are left out and since moves past them, so the snapshot still covers everything it claims to, and the tasks changed least recently are left out.

It carries identifiers and times only: never a finding, a title, a body, a path or a project slug.

Which repository a session is in

A session's repository is found from its working directory through the repo map, exactly as its project is (the longest mapped path the directory lies under, on the session's own host). The repository's name is the last segment of its origin remote - git@host:owner/myapp.git gives myapp - or, with no origin recorded, the last segment of its path. Configure the monitor with the same names. A working directory outside every mapped repository gives null, and so does a name outside the contract's pattern.

A confidential or sealed project's repository is never named, and neither is that of a project locked under peer_auth: their sessions and tasks are still listed - by name or id, with their times and recorded commits - with repo null, the way the metadata feed sends such a project's slug only as a keyed hash. A monitor that matches by time cannot match those sessions; a recorded commit, or one whose message names the session or task, still matches.

What it does not cover

  • A record is an agent's claim. Seamless checks that an id is a full commit id, never that the commit exists or that this session made it. Any caller allowed to end a session or update a task can vouch for a commit on it; the per-call bound keeps an agent from vouching for a whole history in one paste.
  • Agents must pass the ids. Nothing reads git on an agent's behalf. A session that ends through the client's own hook (most Claude Code sessions) records no commits unless the agent called session_end with them; its times and repository still reach the snapshot.
  • It is the record's view, not git's. Commits that never reached a session's or task's record are matched, if at all, by the monitor's own rules - a message naming a listed session or task, or a commit time inside an open session of the same repository.
